summary.text: SPICE aims to better understand combustion by observing flames in microgravity aboard the ISS, and hypothesizes that non-buoyant jet diffusion flames allow study of laminar smoke-point properties.

fuels.text: Methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures were tested.

geometry.text: Burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm.

flow.text: Co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s.

gravity.text: Flames are observed in a microgravity environment aboard the ISS.

measurements.text: Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions.

claims.text: SPICE aims to better understand combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the ISS.
The research hypothesizes that minimizing gravity-driven transport allows study of the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames.
The metadata states the research could help design safer spacecraft environments (stated as a research impact, not as a result).

limitations.text: The metadata states objectives, hypothesis and impacts but no measured result, so no reported observation or finding is recorded.
Only PSI metadata was examined; no document text was processed, so statements are limited to what the metadata fields say.

modeling_resources.description: Candidate data for modeling: SPICE experimental table and numeric raw data files for the measurements listed in the approach (flame height, radiative heat losses, co-flow velocity distributions). No model is claimed.

evidence.excerpt: The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS)
The research hypothesizes that by minimizing gravity-driven transport phenomena scientists can study the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames.
Fuels tested included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures.
burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s
Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions.
